en: The characters of the play;
the male characters: Yaugandharāyaṇa (the Madman)—
Rumaṇvat (Śramaṇaka), the chief minister of the King of Vatsa— the second minister of the King of Vatsa.
Vidūṣaka (Vasantaka):
Haṃsaka, the friend of the King of Vatsa—
Sālaka, the servant of Vatsarāja—
a follower of Yaugandharāyaṇa and a messenger carrying such a message.
Nirmuṇḍaka—
the servant of Yaugandharāyaṇa.
Brāhmaṇa—
The friend of Yaugandharāyaṇa;
Bhaṭa— the bodyguard.
Pradyota (Mahāsena)— kings of Ujjayinī;
Bharatarohaka—
The chief minister of Mahāsena;
Bādarāyaṇa—
the female roles.
Aṅgāravatī— the queen of Mahāsena.
Vijayā—
The Warder of the King of Vatsa.
Act One.
(At the conclusion of the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager enters.)
The Stage Manager: May the exceedingly heroic Mahāsena, together with Vāsavadattā, protect us;
as does the King of Vatsa by name, along with Śakuntalā and Yaugandharāyaṇa.
(Walking around and looking toward the tiring-room) Noble lady! This way, please. (Entering) The Actress—
"Noble sir! Here I am. Director:
"Noble lady! Please sing some piece first. Then, when the audience has been won over by your singing, we shall begin our play. Noble lady, why do you hesitate? Indeed—"
It is sung:

The Actress—Noble sir, today in a dream I saw what appeared to be a banyan tree of the Nyagrodha clan. Therefore, I wish for the noble sir to send some man for the purpose of discerning its auspiciousness. (Today...)
"In a dream, I have seen what appears to be an illness within my kinsmen's family. Therefore, I wish for the Noble One to send some man as a messenger to ascertain the cause of this misfortune.
The Director: "Certainly."
"I shall send a man who is clearly capable of his own welfare.
The Stage Manager: This man is being sent just as Yaugandharāyaṇa [sent his man].
The Stage Manager: Indeed, he sends forth a man, just as Yaugandharāyaṇa does.
(They both exit. Thus ends the prologue. (Then enters Yaugandharāyaṇa together with Sālaka.)
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
Sālaka, be ready! Sālaka: [Does so.]
"Noble sir! Indeed, it is so.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"A truly long journey remains to be traveled."
Sālaka:
I attend upon the noble sir with great affection. (I attend upon the noble sir with great affection.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:—

Alas, he who possesses such friendship will depart with his strength! For why? Because a difficult task must be undertaken toward those who are affectionate, or toward one who recognizes the merits of those who have been honored.
The power acquired by one gradually declines or increases according to the influence of destiny. (3)
Now, since the Master is scheduled to depart tomorrow for the Nāgavana grove situated near the Bamboo Grove, he ought to be attended to beforehand.
Sālaka:
Noble sir, this letter indeed weighs upon me, for upon it depends the very body of our business.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:—
Vijayā! (Entering)
Vijayā: Noble sir, here I am.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:—
Vijayā: Vijaye! Hurry with the letter and the *pratisarā* amulet.
Vijayā: Noble sir! I shall do so. (She exits. (Noble sir! It is done.)
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
Now, has this path been seen by you before?
Sālaka: [Yes.]
"No, never heard before.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"This too is a mark of intelligence. O sir! News has arrived that Pradyota, having presented a dark-colored elephant whose body was concealed by a wild elephant, intends to deceive our master."
Nor, even now, should there be a transgression against our master’s intellect. Oh, how great indeed is Pradyota’s fear of the Vatsa king! The incompetence of an akṣauhiṇī has been made manifest.
Why?
Because his army is clearly vast and numerous, yet it does not have a single purpose.
An army composed of men whose heroism has been reckoned, yet who are not loyal,
will then welcome a ruse at the time of battle; for indeed, the entire host is like a wife when it lacks devotion.
(Entering) Vijayā:

This is indeed a letter. The Queen Mother has said, "Pratisarā, hasten it from the hands of all the ladies-in-waiting. (This is indeed a letter. Pratisarā, [bring it] from the hands of all the ladies-in-waiting.)
"Make haste," said the mother of the husband.
Yaugandharāyaṇa replied: "O Vijayā! Let it be announced to her ladyship that either all the women of the harem, acting with their own hands, should provide a *pratisarā* amulet, or let one be given."
Vijayā:
Noble sir! So be it. (Exit. Noble sir, so be it. (Entering)
Nirmuṇḍaka:— "It is well with the noble sir. (It is well with the noble sir.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:—
Nirmuṇḍaka: How so?
Nirmuṇḍaka:
Noble sir! This Haṃsaka, who has been in attendance at the feet of my master, has arrived.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"Haṃsaka, it is said that one has arrived. Sālaka! Rest now for a moment; you shall go either more quickly or once you have rested.
Sālaka: [listens].
"Noble sir! So be it. (Exit. (Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"My mind is as if filled with anxiety because a single Haṃsaka has arrived, never before separated from his master. Why is that?"
Just as for a man whose kinsmen are scattered, who has gone to another land and returned home,
so indeed is my present state of mental uncertainty.
Shall I hear what is pleasant or indeed unpleasant? || 5 ||
(Then enter Haṃsaka and Nirmuṇḍaka.
Nirmuṇḍaka: Come, come, sir! (Etvetvārya!)
Haṃsaka:
Where, where is the noble sir? (Kutra kutrāryaḥ? Nirmuṇḍaka:—
"There he is, sir; approach him. (Exit. "This noble one stands there; go near him. Haṃsaka—(Approaching) "Is the noble one well? (Sukham āryasya.)
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
Haṃsaka! Has my lord indeed not gone to the Nāga grove?
Haṃsaka: [He has.]
"Noble sir! The master departed this very day.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
Alas, our dispatching him was fruitless! We have been deceived. Now there is hope, or else today itself my life must be abandoned.
"Indeed, my lord is currently holding Haṃsaka.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
By saying "he is currently holding him," you have described a calamity that is not yet severe. Surely the master must be captured!
Haṃsaka:
Well observed by the noble sir! My master has been captured.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: — [continues]

How was the master captured? Alas, sirs! A truly great burden has been cast off from Pradyota’s fortune. From this day forward, the incompetence and infamy of Vatsarāja’s ministers are firmly established. Now, where has Rumaṇvat gone—he who was wise in matters before they arose? And where has the art of horsemanship gone now? For why?
Because it was affectionate, born of friendship, and inherited from his lineage.
A man fit for exertion, one won through his virtues,
one purchased, one lost by enemies due to the density of the fortress,
and one perished in battle because of excessive burden— [all these have been lost]. (6)
Haṃsaka:
If my lord were accompanied by a full retinue of warrior forces, this fault would not exist.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: [Listens.]
"How can one whose retinue consists of an incomplete army of warriors be called a master?
Haṃsaka:
"May the noble sir listen. (May the noble sir listen.)
Yaugandharāyaṇa: You are weary from the journey; please be seated. Haṃsaka: [Sits.]

"Noble sir! Likewise—(sitting down)—let the noble sir listen. When the night still had a portion of dawn remaining, at a time convenient for travel, the Lord crossed the river Narmadā by way of the sandy ford, settled his family in the Bamboo Grove, and set out toward the royal palace along the path of Magadha with a force consisting only of an umbrella and a few attendants, sufficient for the escort of an elephant herd."
"My lord has departed for the elephant forest by a different path, with a force capable of crushing a herd of elephants.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
And then? And then?
Haṃsaka:

Then, when the sun had risen only the distance of an arrow-shot, we traveled as many *yojanas* as it seemed, and having reached Mount Madayantīra just within a *krośa*, we beheld the royal herd—its appearance uneven, like a stone-work half-finished upon the edge of a lake. (Then, when the sun had risen only the distance of an arrow-shot, having traveled as many *yojanas* as it seemed...)
Having reached Mount Madagandhīra in barely a *krośa*, we beheld a herd of elephants with hideous appearance, as if they had been half-finished stone carvings lifted from the mud of a lake.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
And then? And then?
Haṃsaka:

Then, while the troops were gazing [at him] and that herd had become a mass of apprehension, a certain foot-soldier who was the cause of this misfortune approached the Lord himself. (Then, while the troops were gazing [at him] and that herd had become a mass of apprehension, a certain foot-soldier who was the cause of this misfortune approached the Lord himself.)
Yaugandharāyaṇa:

Stop! Did you not say that at a distance of just one *krośa* from here, you saw an elephant with its body concealed by *mallikā* and *sāla* trees, its skin entirely dyed blue except for its nails and tusks?
Haṃsaka: Indeed.
"How indeed was this recognized by my noble lord? This fault has arisen while he was still awake!
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"Haṃsaka! Even for one who is awake, Fate is all too powerful. What happened next?"
Haṃsaka:

Then, having honored that cruel man with the gift of a hundred gold pieces, the King said: "This elephant, named Nīlakuvalaya-tanu, is a master of elephant-training. Therefore, you must remain vigilant regarding this herd. I shall bring that elephant by means of lute-players. (Then, having honored that cruel man with the gift of a hundred gold pieces...)

The King said: "There is this universal monarch's elephant named Nīlakuvalayatanu, who is well-versed in the science of elephant training. Therefore, you must remain vigilant regarding this herd. I shall bring that elephant back, accompanied only by my lute.
Yaugandharāyaṇa—
Now, how was the master neglected by Rumaṇvat at that time?
Haṃsaka:

No, no! Having been propitiated, the minister informed the lord: "It is not even conceivable that you would fail to capture those who have gone to the various quarters, such as Elāpura and the others. [He continued: "Furthermore—"

"Because the border regions are difficult to guard and fraught with imminent dangers, the people living there are shameless and of low birth. Therefore, let us all depart after placing this herd under the supervision of Pādāti-mātra; it is not fitting for the Master to go alone. "No, no! The minister has addressed the Lord with these words:

'Indeed, it is not even conceivable that you would fail to capture the world-elephants such as Airāvaṇa and the rest. Rather, the border territories are difficult to protect and beset by immediate perils. Therein dwell people who are shameless and of ignoble origin.'"
"The people are inhabitants of the borderlands. Therefore, let us all depart together, making this caravan consist of nothing more than foot-soldiers; the master must not travel alone.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"Was the master thus addressed by Rumaṇvat even in the presence of the great multitude? Even so, I desire such devotion to the master that it need not be spoken of. Then [he continued] from there.
Haṃsaka:

Then, having restrained the Minister by an oath sworn upon his own life, [the King] descended from the elephant Nīlabalāhaka, mounted the horse named Sundarapāṭala, and set out on foot together with his attendants, who were slightly behind him as the sun was not yet fully risen. (Then, having restrained the Minister by an oath sworn upon his own life...)
Having dismounted from his elephant and mounted a horse named Sundarapāṭala, the Master departed at sunset with about twenty footmen.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
For victory! Alas! Out of affection, the previous circumstances were not considered. And then? And then?
Haṃsaka:

Then, having traveled what seemed like double the distance, I saw that image of a divine elephant at a spot about a hundred bow-lengths away, indicated by a pair of tusks— seemingly placed there without a body— that appeared to have emerged from the dark greenery of the *sāla* tree’s shade due to its natural luster.
That image of a celestial elephant was indicated by his two tusks, which appeared as if they had been cast from his body and illuminated it, and was seen at a distance of about a hundred bows.
Yaugandharāyaṇa said:
"Haṃsaka! Let it be said that this is our distress. Then, what happened next?
Haṃsaka:
Then the Lord, having dismounted from his horse and approached, paid homage to the deities and took up the lute. Thereupon, a great lion, as if having made a single resolve, appeared from behind him.
Kaṇṭhīrava has arrived.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"Kaṇṭhīrava? And then what happened?"
Haṃsaka:
Then we turned back for the purpose of identifying the lion;
that artificial elephant was met by the chief mahout and his armed followers.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
And then? And then? Haṃsaka: [He continues:]
"Then, having comforted the noble folk by mentioning their names and lineages, [the King said]:

'This is entirely the stratagem of Pradyota; follow me! I shall now, through my prowess, bring to equality the opponent's proposal which was an uneven undertaking. Having spoken thus, the Lord entered that enemy force."
Such indeed is that enemy force.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
"He has entered. Or rather, is it not indeed appropriate?
Abashed at having been deceived, the proud man, relying on his own courage,
being brave and standing on a single path— what else could he do?
Then, from that point onward...
Haṃsaka:

Then, as if playing, following his own whims on the horse Sundarapāṭala, he struck even more than according to his own desire; and because the enemy force was exceedingly large, with all his attendants dejected and scattered as his vigor was being spent, he—protected not by me alone, but certainly by my lord himself—became exhausted from the continuous fighting day after day.

"My lord has fallen into a swoon at this hour, terrible with the scorching sun, his horse having collapsed under many wounds. (Then, as if playing, while striking even more than he intended with a horse that followed his will—a beautiful Pāṭala steed—and while his exertion was greatly increased by the vast number of the enemy's forces, with all his attendants dejected and lost, my lord—no, no, it was my lord himself who protected me—became exhausted from the continuous day-long battle; his horse fell under many blows, and at this time, harsh with the fading sun, my lord fell into a swoon.)"
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
How has my lord fallen into a swoon? What happened next? Haṃsaka: [continues]
Then, as best he could, with rough creepers uprooted from the nearby thicket whose species were unknown, my lord was, as it were, crushed by the constriction of his body like a common man.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
How has my lord been assailed?

He whose broad shoulders are like those of a great elephant-king, who draws his bow with a wide stretch, who is accustomed to wielding the bowstring, and who places arrows upon it from a great distance.
For one who honors the Brahmins, the binding of his two arms— cast down with embraces for the sake of honoring friends during their labors— to a place other than the position of bracelets.
"Now, at what moment did my lord return to life?
Haṃsaka:
"Noble sir! When his sins were stripped of their arrogance."
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
By good fortune, it was your body that was rubbed, not your vital energy. What happened next?
Haṃsaka: [He continues:]

"Now, seeing our lord restored to life, those wicked men have been pursued from all sides, praising the master's prowess in a distorted manner, crying out: 'By him my brother was killed! By him my father! By him my son! By him my friend!'"
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
And then? And then? Haṃsaka: [He continued:]...

And now, another marvel! There, through mutual persuasion, one has resolved to commit an unworthy act. Turning toward the south, having addressed his lord with words that did not cause agitation, and having tied up his hair without restraint, he—desiring to bring forth the force of a blow with his sword by pressing it with his hand—is rushing forward.
(And now, another marvel! There, through mutual persuasion, one has resolved to commit an unworthy act. Turning toward the south, having addressed his lord with words that did not cause agitation...)
Having gathered his hair without ceremony and pressed it down with his hand, Yaugandharāyaṇa, rushing forward with the intent to bring forth the force of a blow with his sword, cried out:
"Haṃsaka! Observe the situation for a moment, until I recover my breath!"
Haṃsaka: Then,
on the ground made slippery by a mass of blood,
that cruel man— his feet having been crushed by his own momentum and his efforts thwarted— fell down, slain.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
This wretch has fallen! O King!
Your kingdom is unassailed by foreign armies and free from the confusion of dharma.
The earth protects the protector who has sought refuge in her.
Haṃsaka:
Then the minister of Pajjota named Sālaṅkāyana—his anger aroused by the first blow from the spear—cried out, "By no means! By no means! Do not act rashly! and went to that place.

He has arrived. (Then, having first been rendered unconscious by a blow from a spear by his master, the minister of Pradyota named Śālaṅkāyana approached that spot, saying, "By no means! By no means! Do not act rashly!
Yaugandharāyaṇa—
And then?
Haṃsaka:
Then, having performed a prostration difficult at such a time, the Master was released by him from the constraint of his body.
[The husband has been liberated.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
Our master is released! Well done, O Śālaṅkāyana! Well done! Indeed, a critical situation can turn even an enemy into a friend. Haṃsaka! You have, as it were, somewhat recovered from your distress.
My mind is troubled. Now, what did that good man do?
Haṃsaka:

Then that noble sir, having spoken many words of consolation with various skillful means, placed him upon a shoulder-cot, saying, "He is incapable of riding or sitting due to the severity of his many wounds."

"The master has been led straight to Ujjayinī. (Then, after the noble ladies had spoken many words of consolation with due courtesy, they placed the master—who was rendered incapable by the severity of his many wounds—upon a litter carried on their shoulders and led him directly to Ujjayinī. Because of Pradyota’s arrogance, the master remains in a state of suffering. (20)
Now, how will that lord of men behold him whom he has never before counted; how will he, whose word is authoritative, hear the words of a mere man?
How will he, who is honored or even oppressed when restrained, maintain his indignation—which is otherwise barren of its object—should he bow down in submission? || 22 ||

These very things have now arrived at the appointed time, yet they are rendered fruitless by the exhaustion of my fortune,
like the auspicious rites of lustration performed for a horse when the battle has already ended.
The female doorkeeper:
Noble sir! Here is Pratisarā.

Portress—Alas!

"Here I go, unfortunate as I am.

Vijayā! You must not hastily announce that the Master has been taken away by her; a mother's heart is fragile with affection and must be protected.
Portress: How shall I announce this now?
Yaugandharāyaṇa: [Silence]
Listen! First, the faults connected with war must be set forth as objects of reflection for those in doubt;
when a matter is uncertain and destruction looms, while grief is deep, the true nature of what ought to be done should be explained.
Portress: I will take it. (Exit.

"Hamsaka! Why have you not gone now with your master?
Hamsaka:
"Noble sir! I indeed intended to go, but I was appointed by Sālaṅkāyana to assist myself."
"Go and report this news to Kauśāmbī. (Noble sir!
I have indeed resolved to favor myself; having been appointed by Sālaṅkāyana, go and report this news to Kauśāmbī.
Yaugandharāyaṇa:—
Is he now wishing to act with hopeless persistence, or is he avoiding the proximity of an affectionate person?
Haṃsaka: Indeed he is. (Exactly so.)
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
He reveals himself out of astonishment, or perhaps it is because everything he has undertaken has been successful. Now, my lord says nothing to me.
Haṃsaka: [He speaks.]

Yes; while circumambulating my lord with a gaze submerged within the water, as if wishing to seize him completely, I was addressed by my lord: 'Go, Yaugandharāyaṇa'—(having spoken thus, he remains silent). Yaugandharāyaṇa replied:
"Let it be spoken freely; this is the command of my lord."

"Do not do so! He says that one must see Yaugandharāyaṇa alone, bypassing the entire circle of ministers.
Haṃsaka: "Indeed! (That is so.)
Yaugandharāyaṇa:

In that case, if my lord indeed deems me worthy of being seen, then I am one whose services have not been requited, who has not yet repaid the sustenance provided by his master, and who has not honored the king with my own service.
Haṃsaka: [Silence.]
"Very well. (Bāḍham.

My lord shall see me concealed by another person.
Whether in the city of an enemy king, in captivity, in the forest, or having met with destruction after death— equally miserable in all these states—
he who, having deceived that king, forms the thought "I have conquered."

This remedy for grief is being offered according to my ability;
this incapacity of women is being voiced by the ministers. (15)

Yaugandharāyaṇa:
What, what? Portress: [She speaks.]

Such is the state of the young prince, who is surrounded by well-wishers. What can be done except through a remedy? Therefore, let the well-wishers be honored and the matter resolved.

For he indeed does not despond in difficulties, nor does he falter when fallen into adversity; he does not succumb to weariness even when separated from his loved ones, nor does he turn back before obstacles.
